L2t: This is the classic coin-exchange recurrence, where a value n can be kept as is or split into parts that are themselves worth more.
L3t: Each f(i) is the larger of i itself and the sum of f(i//2), f(i//3), f(i//4) and f(i//5), with base cases f(0)=0 and f(1)=1, so computing the values in increasing order from a table lets every needed value be looked up.
L4t: Build a table with res[0]=0 and res[1]=1, fill each i up to n with the larger of i and the sum of res at i//2, i//3, i//4 and i//5, then return res[n].
L2f: This recurrence comes from a coin-exchange puzzle, and it is known to be solvable only by trying every possible split of n with brute-force search, since no stored values can be reused.
L3f: The exchange splits a number into only three parts, n/2, n/3 and n/4, so the n/5 term is a typo and should be left out of the sum before comparing it with n.
L4f: The correct approach is to compute f(i) as the larger of i and f(i//2)+f(i//3)+f(i//4), leaving out the n/5 term.
cand_true: Bottom-up table using max(i, sum of the four floor-division terms n/2, n/3, n/4, n/5)
cand_wrong1: Use only three terms n/2, n/3, n/4 and omit n/5
cand_wrong2: Simply return n without any recursion
